summary: Defines an X.509 certificate extension that lets a certificate list the S/MIME capabilities of its owner, complementing the S/MIME Capabilities attribute in signed messages. It gives an optional way to say which cryptographic algorithms an entity supports. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A name tag that also lists which secret languages you can speak. People sending you secure mail can look at it to pick one you understand.

subtitle: Advertise cryptographic capabilities in a certificate extension.

tldr.problem: When sending encrypted S/MIME messages to unknown recipients, the sender has no way to know which cryptographic algorithms they support and must rely on default configuration or out-of-band information.
tldr.mechanism: Define an X.509 certificate extension that lists the subject's S/MIME capabilities, allowing senders to examine the recipient's public key certificate to choose compatible encryption algorithms.
tldr.outcome: Senders can make better algorithm choices based on the recipient's capabilities without requiring prior communication or risky defaults.

today: RFC 4262 is a Standards Track document. The S/MIME Capabilities extension is available for use in certificates but is optional, as applications may choose to ignore it when more reliable capability information is available.

sections.title: The problem of unknown capabilities
sections.content: S/MIME messages are encrypted using the recipient's public key certificate. However, S/MIME capabilities—information about which cryptographic algorithms a recipient supports—are normally communicated through signed attributes in S/MIME messages. When a sender has no prior communication history with a recipient, they do not know what algorithms the recipient can handle. This forces the sender to rely on default configuration, which may be incompatible with the recipient's actual capabilities or security policy.
sections.eli5: You might be the only one who can read a certain type of secret message. But if someone doesn't know that about you yet, they might send it in a way you can't read.

sections.title: The certificate extension
sections.content: This specification adds an S/MIME Capabilities extension to X.509 certificates. The extension uses the exact same data structure (SMIMECapabilities) as the S/MIME Capabilities attribute already defined in RFC 3851. The extension lists cryptographic capabilities such as content encryption algorithms. Certification Authorities should limit the included capabilities to types relevant to the certificate's intended use, and applications processing the extension may ignore any capabilities they do not consider relevant.
sections.eli5: The certificate already has your public key in it. This extension adds a list of what encryption methods you support, right there on the certificate.

sections.title: When capabilities change
sections.content: The S/MIME Capabilities extension states the subject's capabilities at the time the certificate was issued. If those capabilities change during the certificate's lifetime—for instance, if an algorithm becomes considered broken or too weak—the certificate may need to be revoked. However, revocation should only be motivated by actual security concerns, not routine capability updates. The extension must not be marked critical, allowing applications to gracefully ignore it if needed.
sections.eli5: Your certificate's list stays the same until the certificate expires. If your abilities change, you get a new certificate.
